analysis.one_liner: Bans new road building and logging in untouched roadless areas of the national forests.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced with 13 senators behind it but never received a hearing, a vote, or any action in the Senate Energy Committee before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would write the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule into law: no new road construction or timber cutting in the millions of acres of inventoried roadless national forest, with exceptions for safety emergencies, environmental cleanup, highway projects, and existing mineral leases. The bill's stated aims are protecting drinking water watersheds, wildlife habitat, and recreation, while allowing most existing uses to continue unchanged.
analysis.who_benefits: Hikers, hunters, anglers, campers, and other people who use national forests; communities downstream of the more than 354 municipal watersheds that draw drinking water from roadless areas (the bill's findings say roadless protection saves those communities millions of dollars in water filtration costs); and taxpayers, who otherwise fund road building and the Forest Service's large maintenance backlog on its 386,000-mile existing road system.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Forest users and communities drinking from forest watersheds

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits road construction and reconstruction in inventoried roadless areas of the National Forest System, with exceptions for imminent threats to life or property, environmental cleanup actions, safety projects, and federal-aid highways.
Prohibits timber cutting, sale, or removal in roadless areas except for narrow, infrequent exceptions such as endangered-species habitat work and wildfire risk reduction.

The bill's findings state that roadless areas provide drinking water to millions of citizens from more than 354 municipal watersheds and save downstream communities millions of dollars in water filtration costs.

The findings state that protection would affect less than 0.5% of the national timber supply and have a negligible effect on oil and gas production, while leaving access to nearby state, private, and other federal land untouched.

The findings note the Forest Service already carries a maintenance backlog on its existing 386,000-mile road system that costs millions of dollars, and that fires are almost twice as likely in roaded areas as in roadless ones.

analysis.who_pays: Timber companies and road contractors that would lose access to roadless-area timber and Forest Service road-building projects, and energy or mining interests hoping to develop roadless acres — though the bill carves out existing mineral leases, pre-2001 projects, and pending Tongass National Forest projects.

drawbacks.text: Logging and resource-extraction interests would lose access to timber and potential development in roadless areas, which the bill itself concedes affects less than 0.5% of the national timber supply.

The bill locks its protections in place: it says the prohibitions cannot be reconsidered, modified, or terminated through the normal forest planning process, which removes flexibility if local conditions change.
The protections are partial: existing leases, pre-2001 decisions and permits, and pending Tongass National Forest projects are all exempted, so some roadless-area development could continue.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill trades a small, well-documented cost to timber and extraction interests — the bill's own findings put the timber impact under half a percent of national supply — for lasting protection of drinking-water watersheds, wildlife habitat, and recreation across the national forest roadless estate. The main design criticisms are the rigidity of a statutory lock-in that cannot be revised through normal forest planning, and the grandfathering that leaves some development open. On the whole the costs are narrow and the benefits broad and long-lived.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, and the committee never acted on it before that Congress ended, so the bill died there.

narrative.text: Sen. Maria Cantwell introduced the Roadless Area Conservation Act of 2006 on March 2, 2006, joined by 12 Democratic cosponsors including Sens. Bingaman, Boxer, Clinton, Dodd, Harkin, Kerry, Lautenberg, Lieberman, Menendez, and Akaka.
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources.
No further action was taken: the committee never held a hearing, reported the bill, or sent it to the floor, and it died at the end of the 109th Congress in January 2007.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Timber, road-contracting, and extraction interests interested in roadless-area development were better off, since no statutory protection was enacted and roadless areas remained open to whatever management decisions the administration of the day chose to allow. Communities and forest users gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Timber and extraction interests; no protection enacted

for.name: Sen. Maria Cantwell
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor.

for.name: 12 Senate Democratic cosponsors
for.role: Cosponsors including Sens. Bingaman, Boxer, Clinton, Dodd, Harkin, Kerry, Lautenberg, Lieberman, Menendez, and Akaka
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it 13 senators of support at introduction.

against.name: Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup and never reported the bill, leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 13 supporters — the sponsor and 12 cosponsors — were Democrats, and the bill never advanced in a Senate controlled by Republicans in the 109th Congress.

industries.note: The bill bars timber cutting and removal in roadless areas, ending logging there except for narrow habitat and wildfire-risk exceptions. The bill's own findings put the impact at under 0.5% of the national timber supply, and industry gains from the outcome — the bill died.

The bill ends Forest Service road-building and reconstruction in roadless areas, eliminating a source of contract work. The bill's findings argue the public is better served by maintaining the existing 386,000-mile road system than by adding new roads to it.

New development in roadless areas would be barred, but the bill grandfathers mineral leases in effect as of January 12, 2001 and allows roads for their continuation or renewal, and exempts pending Tongass National Forest projects. The findings describe the overall energy impact as negligible.

The bill preserves roadless settings for hiking, camping, hunting, fishing, and other recreation while allowing continued motorized access in many roadless areas, protecting the scenery and habitat that drive forest-based tourism.
